canary: If this tiny bird fell over...
Down here, the deadliest danger was invisible.
A man could breathe it... and never notice.
Scientist John Haldane had found this gas behind deadly mine explosions.
His idea? Send a small bird down first.
Its tiny body breathes so fast, the gas hits it first.
So the men kept glancing at it... all day long.
But here's the part almost nobody knows.
Some cages had their own OXYGEN tank.
Rescue teams carried them into poisoned tunnels.
Shut the little door, open the valve...
and the bird could be REVIVED.
British mines kept canaries until nineteen eighty-six.
A tiny bird... watching over every man underground.
detonator: They used to put EXPLOSIVES on train tracks...
This little metal disc is a railway detonator.
About the size of a coin.
It's strapped to the rail with two soft lead clips.
In thick fog, drivers couldn't see the signals.
Red or green... it all disappeared.
So when a signal showed danger, a fogman placed detonators on the line.
Fogmen stood beside the signals for hours, in the cold.
Usually two or three of them, spaced apart.
A sound no driver could miss... even in total fog.
It meant: DANGER ahead. Slow down... or stop.
Edward Cowper invented it around eighteen forty-one...
and trains still carry detonators today.
A WARNING... loud enough to stop a train.
galveston: This flag warned a whole city that disaster was coming.
Red, with a black square in the middle.
It meant: a STORM is on its way.
Galveston, Texas. September seventh, nineteen hundred.
Weather Bureau chief Isaac Cline watched the waves grow bigger...
and raised the warning flags above the city.
Shops stayed open. People came to the beach to watch the waves.
And Galveston was flat. Its highest point was under nine feet.
The next day, the sky turned black.
Winds over one hundred and thirty miles an hour.
A storm surge over FIFTEEN feet.
The sea swept across the whole island.
At least six thousand people died...
the deadliest natural disaster in American history.
The survivors built a giant seawall... and RAISED their entire city.
That wall still protects Galveston today.
mortsafe: Why would anyone lock a GRAVE... inside an iron cage?
It wasn't built to keep something in.
It was built to keep people OUT!
Medical schools needed bodies to study anatomy...
but almost the only legal supply was executed criminals.
So gangs crept into graveyards at night...
and SOLD the bodies to surgeons!
So they bolted a heavy iron cage over the grave.
And it only had to stay for about six weeks...
until the body was no use to any surgeon.
Then it was lifted off... and moved to the next new grave.
Many were even rented out, by the day!
In eighteen thirty-two, the Anatomy Act gave medical schools a legal supply...
and the body snatchers' trade died away.
But some of these iron cages are still standing in Scottish churchyards today.
antikythera: Divers pulled this lump of bronze from a shipwreck...
In nineteen hundred, sponge divers sheltering from a storm found an ancient wreck.
In nineteen hundred, sponge divers, sheltering from a storm, found an ancient wreck.
and a few crusty lumps that nobody cared about.
Then an archaeologist noticed something in one of them.
A tiny bronze gear wheel... with hand-cut teeth!
From a ship that sank over TWO THOUSAND years ago!
X-ray scans finally revealed what it was.
A hand-cranked machine... that modelled the sky!
Turn the handle, and pointers showed the sun and moon moving.
Even the phases of the moon...
Nothing this complex is known again for more than a thousand years.
fresnel: This giant glass beehive could save a ship... twenty miles away.
Two hundred years ago, lighthouse beams were weak.
Lamps and mirrors wasted much of their light...
and ships often saw the lighthouse far too late.
Then a French physicist, Augustin Fresnel, had a brilliant idea.
Then a French physicist, Augustin Fray-nel, had a brilliant idea.
A normal lens big enough would be far too thick and heavy.
So he cut it into RINGS!
Same curve, a fraction of the glass.
and prisms catch the light that would escape.
It all gets squeezed into one powerful beam!
In eighteen twenty-three, the first one was lit, in the Cordouan lighthouse in France.
In eighteen twenty-three, the first one was lit, in the Cor-doo-on lighthouse in France.
It could be seen... more than twenty miles out to sea!
Soon lighthouses all over the world used them.
A ring of glass... that turned a flame into a lifeline.
